description:
Algorithm A25 `match_glob` — PROTOCOL_SPEC 9.2.3. The single matcher for every glob-dialect pattern-valued value in the specification: `bindings.pattern`, `obs.redaction.sensitive_keys` glob entries, event `event_pattern` / `include_events` / `exclude_events`, and `system.control.reload_module`'s `path_filter`. It is NOT the matcher for ACL rule patterns or `match_modules`, which match module IDs with A08 and are pinned by `pattern_matching.json`.

Two metacharacters and no others: `*` (zero or more characters, crossing `.` and `/`) and `?` (exactly one). Every other character is a literal, `[ ] { } \ ! ^ -` included. The match is anchored to the whole value. Every string is a valid pattern: A25 has no parse phase and MUST NOT raise or skip.

WHY THIS FIXTURE EXISTS (#116, #117). Before v1.37.0 the specification typed these values with the bare word "glob" and named no algorithm, so each SDK delegated to its host library — `pathlib.Path.glob`, `fnmatch`, the `glob` crate, a translated `RegExp` — and inherited that library's dialect. The corpus could not see it: every pattern value in every fixture was `*`, a literal, or leading-star-plus-literal-suffix, which is the one family on which a real glob, a leading-star strip and a first-star removal all coincide. Cases here are therefore chosen by one rule: A CASE EARNS ITS PLACE ONLY IF IT FAILS AGAINST AT LEAST ONE IMPLEMENTATION AS SHIPPED. Of the 30 cases, 11 are marked DISCRIMINATING in their `_why` and name the shipped implementation each one separates; the remaining 19 are marked CONTROL and exist to keep the discriminating cases from being satisfiable by a degenerate matcher.

test_cases._why: CONTROL — the one value every implementation already agrees on.
CONTROL — `*` is zero-or-more, so it matches the empty string.
CONTROL — a pattern with no metacharacter is an exact comparison.
CONTROL — anchored: the pattern must cover the whole value.
CONTROL — no `*`, no `?` — plain equality.
DISCRIMINATING — false wherever `?` is a literal: apcore-rust's event matcher (`*` only), and both non-Python binding loaders, which never look at `?` at all.

CONTROL — `?` is one character, never zero. A `*`-only matcher answers false here too, so this case alone separates nothing — it exists to stop `question_matches_exactly_one_character` from being satisfiable by making `?` match zero-or-more.

DISCRIMINATING — false in apcore-rust's event subscriber matcher, whose own doc comment scopes it to "the subset of fnmatch behaviour the spec fixtures and YAML examples actually exercise", and false in the apcore-rust / apcore-typescript binding loaders.
CONTROL — `?` is exactly one character, so it cannot span `un`.
CONTROL — the pattern is anchored at the start; a leading `x` defeats it.

DISCRIMINATING — the ordinary case a suffix match cannot express. False in apcore-rust's binding loader (`strip_prefix('*')` leaves a pattern that does not begin with `*` unchanged, then `ends_with`) and in apcore-typescript's (`replace('*','')` yields `data.yaml`, then `endsWith`).

DISCRIMINATING — TRUE in apcore-typescript's binding loader today. `replace('*','')` deletes the star WHEREVER it sits, reducing the pattern to `ab.yaml`, and `endsWith` then accepts a file the pattern is anchored away from. No glob dialect matches this.
CONTROL — the `path_filter` fixture's own value family. Present as a control, not as coverage.

CONTROL — the default `bindings.pattern` family — leading star plus literal suffix, the one shape on which a real glob, a leading-star strip and a first-star removal all coincide. This is the family the whole corpus was drawn from, which is why it caught nothing.

DISCRIMINATING — pins the search STRATEGY, not the syntax. Two matchers can both honour `*` and `?` and still disagree here, which is why 9.2.3 specifies A25 as an algorithm rather than as a character set.
CONTROL — the interior star matches zero characters; the final segment still has to be found.
CONTROL — one character cannot satisfy both the head and the tail segment.

DISCRIMINATING — `glob::Pattern::new("a**b")` is an ERROR in apcore-rust ("recursive wildcards must form a single path component"), so `path_filter` refuses a request the other two serve. Under A25 the empty interior segment is a no-op and `**` is not a construct.
CONTROL — `**` widens nothing; the tail segment is still required.

DISCRIMINATING — `glob::Pattern::new("a[b")` is an ERROR in apcore-rust ("invalid range pattern"). Under A25 there is no parse phase: every string is a pattern, so an unbalanced bracket matches itself instead of failing the request.
DISCRIMINATING — TRUE in apcore-python's binding loader, whose `Path.glob` reads `[ab]` as a character class. A25 has no classes.

DISCRIMINATING — false in ALL THREE class-aware matchers — `fnmatch`, `glob::Pattern` and apcore-typescript's `_globToRegExp`, which passes `[ab]` through to a `RegExp` verbatim. Stated from the positive side so an implementation cannot satisfy `bracket_is_a_literal_not_a_class` merely by rejecting the pattern.

DISCRIMINATING — TRUE in apcore-python (`fnmatch`) and apcore-rust (`glob::Pattern`), which both read `[!p]` as "any character except p". Under A25 there is no negation, so this redacts nothing — and, crucially, the operator finds that out at the first test rather than never.

DISCRIMINATING — TRUE in apcore-typescript today: `_globToRegExp` passes `[!p]` verbatim into a `RegExp`, where it means "`!` or `p`". The meaning is INVERTED, not weakened — TypeScript redacts the one field the other two deliberately exclude, and leaks the ones they catch (#117 §1).
CONTROL — brace expansion is in no dialect here; all three current matchers already agree.
CONTROL — there is no escape character. The pattern is `a`, `\`, `*`, `b`, so a literal backslash is required in the value. All three current matchers agree.
CONTROL — the same pattern against a value that does contain the backslash.
CONTROL — `.` is a literal, not a regex wildcard. All three current matchers escape it; the case pins the property so a future glob-to-RegExp translation cannot drop the escape silently.
CONTROL — `*` spans `.`; A25 is not segment-aware, and agrees with A08 on this point.

CONTROL — `*` spans `/` too. A25 is a string matcher, not a path matcher — a distinction that matters because `bindings.pattern` is applied to a FILENAME (5.12.6) and never to a path, so an implementation must not reach for a path-aware library and inherit its non-recursive `*`.
